title: Algorithm-guided experimentation for self-driving laboratories
contribution: Talk deck that re-runs the 2013 DFO benchmark with 39 free codes on the same 502 problems against BARON/LINDOGlobal optima, ranks BAM first (70%, union 79%, 13 dominating and 6 essential solvers) and runs the top five on an in-silico flow reactor as the route to algorithm-guided critical-mineral experiments.
problem_entry: Application pull (critical-mineral separation in a self-driving lab, p. 2) entered through a benchmarking question: performance depends on problem type, dimension and budget, studies disagree and few benchmarks exist against a growing literature (p. 9, chart).
key_idea: No new algorithm: a benchmark-to-lab pipeline (39 codes on 502 problems, pp. 10-14; dominating/essential sets, pp. 22-23, 29; top five on a 4-input, 3-objective in-silico reactor, pp. 24-28; then BAM in the lab, p. 29); BAM is placed among 'Branch-without-bounds' codes but not described (p. 17, chart).
assumptions: Bound-constrained black boxes, same bounds mostly [-10000, 10000] where a solver needs them (p. 14); dimension and convexity x smoothness classes (pp. 12-13, image); no noise in the setup (p. 14); reactor with box-bounded tau, conc_A, equiv_B, T and objectives STY, E-factor, weighted sum (p. 25, image).
proof_devices: analysis device, not a proof: union ('Solvable') curve of the solver set and dominating/essential solver sets, essential ones marked in red (pp. 20-23, 29)
experiments: Defaults via non-intrusive interface, same bounds and starts, 2500 iterations and 18000 CPU s (BayesOpt, DAKOTA/EGO excepted), BARON/LINDOGlobal optima, 0.01 or 1% tolerance, median of 10 random starts with 13 solvers excepted (p. 14); at 2,500 evaluations BAM ~0.70, MCS ~0.50 (p. 15, chart), BAM ~0.83 and ~0.60 on n in [10,30] and [31,300] (p. 19, chart), union 79% (p. 20); reactor: five codes reach the same plateau in 50-100 evaluations, BAM last on STY and weighted sum (pp. 27-28, charts); no versions or hardware; only BAM's curves differ from S277 (54%).
positioning: Continues Rios & Sahinidis 2013, Ploskas & Sahinidis 2022, Amaran et al. 2016 (p. 3); shows the 2013 result chart led by TOMLAB codes (p. 10, chart) and camel6 plots of the 2013 solver set (pp. 7-8, image), while the free-software rule drops the TOMLAB codes from the new run (p. 11); reactor from Hone et al. 2017 and Felton et al. 2021 (p. 24); BAM not identified as the presenters' or firm's solver (pp. 1-31).
writing: Question slide, protocol slide, one-bullet headline repeated in the conclusions (pp. 9, 14, 20, 29); citation counts of popular methods (p. 5) before a covering set without GA, annealing or swarm codes (pp. 23, 29), contrast unstated; 'convergence rates' for success rates (p. 29); '50 evaluations' claimed although BAM plateaus later (pp. 27-28).
limits_future: No limitations slide; next step BAM on critical-mineral separation (p. 29); unstated limits visible in the setup: bound constraints only, no noise, no hold-out for the winner, no versions, 2013 commercial leaders excluded (pp. 10-14).

title: A large-scale benchmarking of deterministic and stochastic black-box optimization algorithms
contribution: Talk deck (28 Oct 2025) refreshing Rios & Sahinidis 2013: 39 free DFO codes on the same 502 problems with the 2013 success rule (median of 10 runs within 1% or 0.01 of the global optimum), BAM first at 54% with a 72% union and a minimal irreducible 12-solver dominating set, plus an in-silico reactor demonstration.
problem_entry: State of benchmarking: performance depends on problem type, dimension and budget, studies reach inconsistent conclusions; question of a large unified reproducible suite; their own 2013 study and chart restated as the baseline (pp. 2-3).
key_idea: Re-run the 2013 benchmark with 39 implementations restricted to software free for academic use, split 26 deterministic / 13 stochastic and 21 global / 18 local (p. 4, image), results per family panel and per dimension class, summarized by a minimal irreducible dominating set (pp. 7-14).
assumptions: Same 502 problems by dimension (20/26/24/30% for n in {1,2}, [3,9], [10,30], [31,300]) and convexity x smoothness (p. 5, image); bounds and noise not mentioned on this deck (pp. 5-6).
proof_devices: analysis device, not a proof: success rule f(y) <= max(1.01 f(x*), f(x*) + 0.01) on the median of 10 runs, as in 2013 (p. 6; S001 p. 21)
analysis device, not a proof: 'Solvable' union curve and minimal irreducible dominating solver set (pp. 12-14)
experiments: Up to 2,500 evaluations, 10 starts where accepted, 141,564 instances, 5 h CPU cap per instance (p. 6; 10 CPU min per run in 2013, S001 p. 22); at 2,500 evaluations BAM ~0.54, MCS ~0.50 (p. 7, chart); on n in [3,9] NOMAD ~0.60 and MCS ~0.59 ahead of BAM ~0.53 (p. 10, chart); BAM 54%, union 72%, 94/78/74/52% per dimension class (pp. 12-13); 12-solver set (p. 14); reactor plateau in 50-100 evaluations with BAM last on yield (p. 15, chart); no versions, hardware or seeds.
positioning: Explicit continuation of Rios & Sahinidis 2013 (p. 3); reactor from Hone et al. 2017 and Felton et al. 2021 (p. 15); the free-software rule removes the TOMLAB codes that led the 2013 chart (pp. 3-4), so the win is relative to the free set.
writing: Short deck: question, protocol with formula, three headline bullets, conclusions with future work (pp. 2, 6, 12, 16); 'deterministic and stochastic' realized as the 26/13 pool split (p. 4, image); 'convergence rates' for success rates (p. 16); hidden grouped solver list in the text layer of p. 4.
limits_future: Future work only: more state-of-the-art DFO solvers and realistic science and engineering problems (p. 16); unstated: no hold-out, no versions, commercial 2013 leaders excluded, BAM's relation to the authors (pp. 3-4, 12).

title: New proofs of exact LP reformulations for binary polynomial optimization with bounded treewidth
contribution: Gives two new proofs (an extreme-point perturbation argument and a primal-dual complementary-slackness construction whose dual is the tree-decomposition dynamic program) that the O(k2^d) LP for binary polynomial optimization with treewidth d is exact, and derives that its representation is TDI.
problem_entry: Revisits a known theorem (Laurent 2009; Bienstock and Munoz 2018) whose proofs are inductive on tree-decomposition nodes; motivation from BPO's NP-hardness, MINLPLib autocorrelation instances and QUBO (pp. 1-2, 4-5).
key_idea: A new form of the standard LP: bag-wise convex-combination multipliers, projection of the lifted w variables, and row operations that leave each multiplier in exactly one equation per parent-child block with one convexity row at the root; both proofs run on it (pp. 5-12).
assumptions: Binary variables, polynomial objective and constraints, associated graph of treewidth d with a known tree decomposition of k nodes (pp. 1, 4-5); finding the decomposition not discussed; TDI for integral objectives (p. 15).
proof_devices: exact bag-wise integer program from clique containment in a bag of the tree decomposition (pp. 6-7)
Claim 1 by reverse induction over the iterations of a row-operation algorithm (Algorithm 1, pp. 10-11)
midpoint perturbation of a fractional extreme point with epsilon the smallest fractionality, propagated root to leaves via Observation 1 (pp. 12-13)
dual written as a min-recursion (the DP), explicit primal-dual construction and complementary slackness (pp. 13-15)
TDI corollary from integral optimal duals for integral objectives (p. 15)
positioning: Theorem credited to Laurent 2009 and Bienstock and Munoz 2018; Wainwright and Jordan 2004 for RLT up to treewidth degree; Faenza et al. 2022, Del Pia and Khajavirad 2024, Cifuentes, Dey and Xu 2024 related; Martin, Rardin and Campbell 1990 for polyhedral DP; prior proofs restated, not criticized (pp. 2, 4).
writing: Short note with contributions in the abstract and end of Section 1 and one running example through Examples 1-6; the example's b1b4 coefficient changes from -5 (pp. 5, 8) to +1 (pp. 9, 12, 15) and Example 3 mislabels bag indices (p. 9).
limits_future: Theory only; claimed uses for cutting planes and sensitivity analysis are not pursued (p. 2); no conclusion, limitations or future-work section (ends at Corollary 2, p. 15).

method_links.note: an exact polyhedral LP is valued for exactness, TDI and O(k2^d) size; nothing is timed, so strength at speed appears only as a size bound
no solver, library or computation: Georgia Tech theory with Dey outside the lab-notebook route on this evidence

new_pattern_candidates.evidence: the LP dual is the dynamic program over the tree decomposition; duals by leaf-to-root recursion, primals by root-to-leaf choice, complementary slackness, TDI as a by-product

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: block normal form before integrality proofs
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: row operations make each multiplier appear once per parent-child block, which enables both the perturbation and the duality proof

transferable: Prove an LP integral by constructing both solutions: duals by a leaf-to-root recursion (the DP), primals by a root-to-leaf choice along active dual constraints; complementary slackness closes the proof, and integral duals for integral objectives give TDI (pp. 13-15).

Before a midpoint (perturbation) argument, use row operations so that each variable appears in exactly one equation per block; perturbations then pass from parent to child one block at a time (pp. 10-13).
When a theorem is known only through an inductive proof, look for a direct duality or extreme-point proof that may yield extra structure such as TDI (pp. 4-5, 15).
Carry one tiny running example through every reformulation and recheck its data at each appearance (pp. 5-15).
coauthors: Sourabh K. Choudhary (first author), Santanu S. Dey

quotes.text: The dual to the LP is the DP formulation for solving such problems over known tree decompositions.
The central ingredient in both proofs is a new reformulation of the standard LP associated with these results.

title: Water network design and operation optimization: Leveraging approximations
contribution: Proves that a standard four-interval piecewise-linear MILP of the Hazen-Williams friction always yields MINLP-feasible produced-water designs with near-optimality bounds paid in pump costs, and introduces continuous-variable diving (approximate, solve the MILP, shrink domains around the solution) that improves three of nine best-known urban water network solutions.
problem_entry: Hazen-Williams friction (q^1.85) named as the source of nonconvexity; primal solutions are the bottleneck for global solvers on produced-water networks; MILP approximations in the literature lack guarantees, and direct PWL fails for urban design (pp. 1-3, 14).
key_idea: PWL secants overestimate friction, so relief valves absorb the error and every PWL solution maps to a feasible MINLP solution at no higher cost, while the reverse loss is bounded by pump costs (Props 3.1-3.3, pp. 10-14); for urban design, fit one least-squares line on the current box, solve the MILP, recentre and shrink the box by eta until the discrepancy is within tolerance (pp. 14-16).
assumptions: Fixed topology, one diameter per arc, binary flow directions, big-M pressure rules, flows in [0, Qmax] (pp. 4-8); Prop 3.2 needs chordless cycles and slack pressures at an MINLP optimum, said to hold but not shown where BARON found no upper bound (pp. 11, 18); Prop 4.1 needs univariate Lipschitz nonlinearities (p. 16).
proof_devices: PWL-to-MINLP map: recompute friction and move the difference into the relief-valve variable (Prop 3.1, p. 10)

MINLP-to-PWL map by cycle-wise residual correction: one-way-flow cycles must contain a pump, mixed cycles get a valve on a counter-flow arc, then a global pressure shift D from the sources (Prop 3.2, pp. 11-13)
cost accounting of the corrections in pump terms, read as pump operating costs (pp. 13-14)
iteration bound ceil(log(2 D0 gamma/eps)/log(eta/2)) via a point where the least-squares line meets f and Lemma 1 bounding the fitted slope by the Lipschitz constant (pp. 16, 27)
experiments: i7-1165G7, Gurobi 12.0, BARON 25.2 (p. 16); 4 PARETO case studies with stress and pump-cost factors and 9 MINLPLib urban instances (pp. 16-17); PWL gaps 0.1-0.3% vs MILP-relaxation bounds while BARON found no upper bound in 3 h on Permian and Treatment (Table 3, p. 18); CVD better than best known on 3 of 9, gaps 0-16.1% to BARON bounds, fails on New York with one segment (Table 6, p. 19); PARETO CVD gaps 0.2-2.2% except Small 24-30% (Table 8, p. 20); sensitivity to eta and MILP time limits (Tables 10-11, pp. 21-22); sample count P and BARON options not reported.
positioning: Bragalli et al. 2012 frames the urban problem; recent MILP approaches (Shao et al. 2024, MILPnet) and Alperovits-Shamir 1977 lack guarantees; Dey and Gupte 2015 as the model of a guaranteed approximation; mesh refinement and diving heuristics as nearest methods; best-known values from minlp.org (Grossmann and Lee 2024) and Rajagopalan 2018; BARON is the named comparator (pp. 2-4, 14, 19).
writing: Two contribution bullets, propositions announced in words and followed by interpreting Remarks (pp. 3-4, 10-14); overstatements against own tables ('consistently delivers near-optimal solutions for all', 'much faster than BARON', 'eta = 3 is optimal', New York 'optimal' with Delta2 = 0 despite a 29% gap to BARON's bound) (pp. 4, 19-22).
limits_future: Stated: chords conceivable, direct PWL fails for urban design, one-segment CVD fails on New York, large eta causes infeasibility (pp. 4, 13, 19, 21); future: CVD on other MINLPs with continuous nonlinearities (p. 23); unstated: 'general-purpose' claim tested only on the univariate signpower term, no code or modified-instance release mentioned.

method_links.note: MILP approximations solved by Gurobi replace the MINLP; PWL accuracy-versus-speed trade-off stated and four intervals kept; the MILP without nonlinear constraints gives tight lower bounds, stronger than BARON's on Treatment
initial flow bounds by minimizing and maximizing each flow over the linear relaxation before the heuristic starts
CVD's domain reduction is heuristic, recentred on the MILP solution and not nested; it serves feasibility, not bounding
every heuristic value set against best-known solutions and a valid lower bound (BARON's or the MILP relaxation's)

CVD defaults (eta = 3, time setting 2) picked as best on the same nine instances that carry the headline; at eta = 2.5, eta = 4 or time setting 1 none of the three improvements survives; own advice to tune on a smaller instance not applied; New York called optimal without a supporting bound (Heuristic 7); student-first paper, weak evidence on Sahinidis's own practice
BARON 25.2 used as external baseline and bound source, not as the lab notebook: no ablation inside BARON, CVD not reported as a BARON component, protocol set per paper

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: slack-absorbed approximation with a device-priced bound
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: secant overestimation absorbed by relief valves makes the PWL a restriction; the reverse loss is bounded by the cost of pumps that would compensate the error
pump costs multiplied by 5, 10 and 15 because the propositions say the gap depends on them; gaps grow as predicted and stay below 5%
least-squares linearization on the current box, MILP solve, domain recentred and shrunk by eta, with an iteration bound in log(2 D0 gamma/eps)/log(eta/2)

transferable: Show that an approximation is a restriction by mapping its solutions to feasible ones through a slack device, then bound the reverse loss by the cost of a compensating device (pp. 10-14).
Stress-test exactly the parameter that appears in your error bound and check that the gap moves as the bound predicts (p. 17; Table 5, p. 18).

Set each MILP time limit by the root-LP solve-time class and publish the sensitivity of results to that rule and to the shrink factor, infeasible runs included (pp. 19, 21-22).
